title: Linda: Less Is More
hook: The detailed story sounds truer, even as every added clause makes the probability smaller.
counterintuition: The richer story can be less likely. When added detail makes an option more plausible but mathematically narrower, prefer the broader category first.
tryThisNow: Find one option today with an added detail after the word and. Cross out the detail, compare the broader category, then decide which is more probable.
keyTakeaway: Do not let plausibility outrank probability; a category plus extra detail cannot be more likely than the broader category alone.

breakdown.fastRead:
An airport agent hears that a missing bag belongs to a violinist and contains a black concert dress. The story feels stronger than plain bag belongs to passenger. It is also narrower.

More detail can mean less probability.

The conjunction fallacy happens when a specific story feels more likely than the broader category it belongs inside. The correction is to compare width. Bag owner is broader than bag owner and touring violinist. The detailed version may sound better, but it has more conditions to satisfy.
breakdown.deepRead:
A blood bank scheduler hears two descriptions. First: the donor is compatible. Second: the donor is compatible and available for a last-minute emergency run. The second sounds more helpful, more vivid, and closer to the need. But it cannot be more probable than compatibility alone.

Linda is the clean warning: a detailed story can become more plausible while becoming mathematically narrower.

The mind confuses plausibility with probability because detail makes a story easier to imagine. A person with a cause, a role, a habit, or a vivid motive feels like someone real. The broader category feels bland. But probability counts conditions. Every added condition can only keep the probability the same or reduce it. It cannot make the combined event more likely than one of its parts.

This is not gullibility. It is a conflict between story sense and set logic. Story sense rewards coherence and detail. Probability asks how many things must be true at once. The more conjuncts you add, the more ways the story can fail.

A jazz rehearsal room can show it without any statistics jargon. The band thinks the substitute pianist is late because his train stalled and he stopped for reeds. That story feels more human than simply late because of transit. But train stalled and stopped for reeds is narrower than late because of transit. The vivid extra detail should not increase the probability estimate.

A good story can be a bad probability judgment.
breakdown.fullRead:
The mind likes details because details make a story breathe. A person becomes easier to picture. A cause feels closer. A category turns into a scene. That is useful for memory, empathy, and explanation. It is dangerous when the question is probability.

Linda shows the switch. The richer description makes one combined category feel more fitting than a broader one. But a combined category must fit inside the broader category. If someone is a bank teller and active in a cause, that person is still a bank teller. The added detail can make the story more plausible to imagine, but it cannot make the combined event more likely than the base category.

Ask the set question: Which option contains the other?

That question cuts through the spell. Passenger with bag contains passenger with bag and unusual profession. Defective part contains defective part and night-shift assembly. Late checkout contains late checkout and deliberate fee avoidance. If the detailed option sits inside the broad option, the broad option must be at least as probable.

A city pothole hotline gives the everyday form. A caller reports a deep hole near a school. The detailed story says a delivery truck caused it during morning drop-off. That sounds plausible because it has motion, motive, and place. But pothole near school is broader than pothole caused by delivery truck during morning drop-off. The delivery detail may guide investigation. It should not make the detailed explanation more probable than the broader report.

A hotel night audit shows the accounting version. A cash discrepancy could be a missing paid-out slip. Or it could be a missing paid-out slip and a clerk hiding a minibar refund. The second story may explain more feelings in the room, especially if the clerk seemed nervous. But it is narrower. The color-grading reference card labeled detail on the postmortem board reminds the team that every added condition costs probability.

This is not an argument against detail. Detail can increase diagnosticity when it discriminates between categories. If the question is which explanation fits after evidence appears, detail may matter a lot. The warning is about ranking probability when one option literally includes another plus extra conditions. In that case, the broader option wins before the story begins.

The limit is that real decisions often mix probability with consequence. A narrow event may be less likely but more serious, and therefore worth guarding against. That does not make it more probable. Keep likelihood and severity in separate columns.

When a story gets richer, count the conditions. Probability shrinks when the doorway narrows.

questions.prompt: A baggage agent thinks a claim is more likely because the passenger says the bag contains a violinist's concert dress. Which option is mathematically broader?
choices: The passenger owns the bag.
The passenger owns the bag and is a violinist with a concert dress inside.
The passenger is lying about the contents.
questions.explanation: Ownership contains the detailed ownership-plus-violinist story. The detail may aid verification, but it cannot make the narrower event more probable than the broad category.

questions.prompt: A blood bank scheduler says a donor is more likely to be compatible and available than merely compatible because the emergency story fits the need. What is the error?
choices: Availability should never matter in scheduling.
The combined condition is being judged more probable than one of its parts.
Compatibility is impossible to estimate.
questions.explanation: Compatible and available is narrower than compatible. Availability matters operationally, but it cannot increase the probability of the combined condition above the broader condition.

questions.prompt: A band thinks a pianist is late because his train stalled and he stopped to buy reeds. Another option is simply that transit delayed him. Which should rank higher on probability alone?
choices: Transit delayed him and he stopped to buy reeds.
Both are equally likely because the second is more vivid.
Transit delayed him.
questions.explanation: The broader transit-delay category includes the narrower reeds story. Vividness increases plausibility, not probability. Evidence for reeds can be added later.

questions.prompt: A pothole caller says a delivery truck caused the hole near a school. The city must log the most probable category first. What should it log?
choices: Pothole near school.
Pothole near school caused by a delivery truck during drop-off.
False report because the delivery story is too detailed.
questions.explanation: The broad hazard is more probable than the same hazard plus one specific cause. The delivery story is useful as a lead, not as the higher-probability category.

questions.prompt: An intake team thinks an animal was more likely injured by falling from a tree and being struck by a bicycle than injured by a fall. Why is that wrong?
choices: Bicycles cannot be part of injury stories.
The fall-plus-bicycle story adds a condition and is therefore narrower than fall injury.
Vivid stories should always be rejected.
questions.explanation: The added bicycle condition makes the story easier to picture but harder to satisfy. The issue is probability width, not whether bicycles are possible or vivid stories are banned.

questions.prompt: A night audit trainee says the cash discrepancy is probably a missing paid-out slip and a hidden minibar refund. Claudia says missing paid-out slip alone is more probable. Why?
choices: Because minibar refunds never happen.
Because clerks should not be accused at night.
Because broader categories have more ways to be true.
questions.explanation: The broad slip category includes the slip-plus-refund story. The refund may become plausible with evidence, but probability falls when conditions are added.

questions.prompt: A diagnosis sounds more likely when the clinician adds three specific symptoms to a rare condition. Which check guards against the conjunction fallacy?
choices: Ask whether the detailed condition is contained inside a broader condition and compare their probabilities.
Prefer the detailed story because it contains more medical information.
Ignore all symptoms and use only base rates.
questions.explanation: The containment check exposes when a detailed conjunction is being ranked above its broader category. Details can be diagnostic, but they cannot make a subset more probable than its superset.

questions.prompt: A product team says a user is likely to churn and write a public complaint because her last ticket was angry. Which category is broader?
choices: The user will churn and write a public complaint.
The user will churn.
The user will stay.
questions.explanation: Churn alone is broader than churn plus public complaint. The angry ticket may raise both estimates, but the combined event cannot outrank the broader one on probability.

questions.prompt: A manager says the more detailed version of an incident must be more likely because it explains more facts. What should you ask?
choices: Which option is more interesting?
Which option sounds more like our usual stories?
Which option contains the other?
questions.explanation: Containment identifies the broader category. Interesting and familiar stories can increase plausibility while lowering probability if they add conditions.

reviewCards.front: A story becomes more detailed and more believable. What probability question should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask which option contains the other. If the detailed story is a subset of the broad category, it cannot be more probable than the broad category.

reviewCards.front: Why does Linda feel persuasive even when the math says no?
reviewCards.back: The added detail makes the story more plausible and coherent. Probability counts conditions, so the detailed conjunction is narrower despite sounding better.

reviewCards.front: A report says event A and cause B happened. Event A alone is also an option. Which ranks higher on likelihood?
reviewCards.back: Event A alone ranks at least as high because it includes every A-and-B case plus A cases without B. Added cause can guide investigation, not outrank the broader event.
Detail matters when it is evidence that changes the likelihood of competing broad categories. It still cannot make a conjunction more probable than one of its required parts.

reviewCards.front: How do you separate probability from consequence in a narrow event?
reviewCards.back: Keep likelihood and severity in separate columns. A narrow event can be less likely but more serious, which may justify planning without making it more probable.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is checking category width. When a detailed story sounds more likely, ask whether it is actually a narrower conjunction inside a broader category.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an explanation contains and, then compare it with the broader explanation before ranking probability.
If a detailed diagnosis story feels compelling, then ask whether the broad condition alone must be at least as likely.
If a client's story gains details that make it feel truer, then separate verification value from probability width.
If a failure story names event plus specific cause, then log the event category first and treat the cause as a hypothesis.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, find one statement with a combined event. Write the broad category above it and mark which one is mathematically wider.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review three explanations you accepted. Circle every added condition and ask whether plausibility made a narrower event feel more probable.
